The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], each weak derivative $\partial_iv_i$ is in $L^2$, so their finite sum $\operatorname{div}v$ is in $L^2(D)$.
For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$, each component derivative has integral zero by one-dimensional integration along its coordinate, hence $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

By [A1, F1], choose $v_n\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$ converging to $v$ in $H^1$. Then $\operatorname{div}v_n\to\operatorname{div}v$ in $L^2$ by [F2]. Applying [F3] to the difference shows their integrals converge; the zero integrals in step 1.2 therefore give $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

derivations.claim: For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$, expanding the symmetric gradient gives $2|\varepsilon(v)|^2=|\nabla v|^2+\sum_{i,j}\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j$ pointwise.

For each $i,j$, apply [F3] to $h=v_i\partial_i v_j$, which is compactly supported and smooth. The product rule gives $\int_D\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j=-\int_Dv_i\partial_j\partial_iv_j$. Summing in $j$ and using equality of mixed derivatives gives $-\sum_i\int_Dv_i\partial_i(\operatorname{div}v)$. Apply [F3] again to $h=v_i\operatorname{div}v$ and sum in $i$ to obtain $\sum_i\int_D(\partial_iv_i)\operatorname{div}v=\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: Fix one graph chart, with Lipschitz constant $L$, and a smaller horizontal ball $C$ whose closure lies in its base. Shrink its radius $r$ until the chart's upper height $H_{\rm chart}$ satisfies $H_{\rm chart}-\sup_C\varphi>4(L+1)r$. Choose $c$ with $\sup_C\varphi+3(L+1)r<c<H_{\rm chart}-(L+1)r$ and $0<\rho<r$. Then the closed ball $\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$ stays in the cylinder. Set $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ with $c+\rho<H<H_{\rm chart}$.

If $x\in U$, $z\in\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$, and $w=(1-t)x+tz$ with $0<t<1$, then $z'\in C$ and convexity keeps $w'\in C$. Since $|z'-x'|\le2r$, Lipschitz continuity gives $\varphi(w')\le\varphi(x')+2Lrt$. Also $c-\rho>\sup_C\varphi+2Lr$, so $w_d>(1-t)\varphi(x')+t(c-\rho)>\varphi(x')+2Lrt\ge\varphi(w')$, and $w_d<H$ by convexity of the vertical interval. Thus $w\in U$; the endpoints belong to $U$ as well, proving star-shapedness with respect to the closed ball.

The boundary $\partial D$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1]. At any $p\in\partial D$, a chart containing $p$ writes the boundary locally as $x_d=\varphi(x')$, with $p_d=\varphi(p')$ strictly below the chart's upper height. Shrinking a horizontal ball $C$ about $p'$ makes its closure lie in the chart base and makes the height-gap inequality of step 1.1 hold; the choices there then produce a patch $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ star-shaped with respect to its selected closed ball by step 2.1. Since $p$ lies inside the chart and inside the open set with $x'\in C$ and $x_d<H$, there is an ambient open ball $N$ about $p$ whose closure lies in that chart and open set. For every $x\in N\cap D$, the chart description gives $x_d>\varphi(x')$, so $x\in U$ and $N\cap D\subset U$. Let $\mathscr N$ be the family of all pairs $(N,U)$ obtained this way from the finite chart atlas and admissible local choices; the preceding existence argument shows that its first components cover $\partial D$, without choosing a patch simultaneously for every boundary point. Compactness supplies a finite subfamily $(N_i,U_i)$, $1\le i\le m$, whose neighborhoods cover $\partial D$. Their union is an open neighborhood of the compact boundary, so some relative collar $\{x\in D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)<\delta\}$ lies in that union and hence in $\bigcup_{i=1}^mU_i$. The remainder $K_\delta=\{x\in\overline D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)\ge\delta\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1], and is contained in $D$ because every point of $\overline D\setminus D$ lies on $\partial D$. Finitely many balls with closures in $D$ cover $K_\delta$; each ball is convex and star-shaped with respect to a smaller concentric ball. Together these sets form a finite star-shaped cover of $D$.

The intersection graph is connected: if it split into two nonempty graph components, the unions of the corresponding open sets would be disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets whose union is $D$, contradicting connectedness. Each tree-edge intersection is nonempty and open, so it contains a ball. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported in that ball. Its integral is strictly positive; dividing by that integral gives $\psi_{ij}\in C_c^\infty(U_i\cap U_j)$ with integral one.

conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, star-shaped with respect to a closed ball $\overline B(a,\rho)\subset U$. Choose $\omega\in C_c^\infty(B(a,\rho))$ with $\int\omega=1$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(U)$, initially define the vector-valued integral
$$ (\mathcal B_U f)(x)=\int_U f(y)(x-y)\int_0^1\omega\!\left(y+\frac{x-y}{t}\right)\frac{dt}{t^{d+1}}\,dy. $$
The inner integral is first interpreted for $t>0$; its locally integrable kernel, support and divergence identity are proved in the following lemma. All data and fields here are real. This definition makes no finite-quadrature or numerical-algorithm claim.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Under $x=y+t(z-y)$, the inner pairing contains $t^{-1}\partial_j\phi(z)\zeta(y+t(z-y))$. Integration by parts in $z$ changes its integral to $-\int\phi(z)\partial_j\zeta(y+t(z-y))dz$; the factor $t^{-1}$ has canceled. Its absolute value is at most $\|\phi\|_1\|\nabla\zeta\|_\infty$, uniformly in $y,t$. The omitted $t$-integral is therefore bounded by $\epsilon\|f\|_1\|\phi\|_1\|\nabla\zeta\|_\infty$, so the distributional limit exists.

For $\epsilon<t<1/2$, Fourier transform in $x$ and use $x=y+t(z-y)$, whose Jacobian is $t^d$. The factor $t^{-d}$ cancels the Jacobian and $\partial_{x_j}\phi(z)=t^{-1}\partial_{z_j}\phi(z)$. Integration by parts in $z$ gives $\widehat{\partial_j\phi}(t\xi)=2\pi it\xi_j\widehat\phi(t\xi)$ by [F1]; the remaining $y$ integral is $\widehat f((1-t)\xi)$. Hence the truncated transform is $2\pi i\xi_j\int_\epsilon^{1/2}\widehat\phi(t\xi)\widehat f((1-t)\xi)dt$. On each compact set of $\xi$, the integrand is uniformly bounded near $t=0$, so the truncated Fourier transforms converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to the displayed integral. Step 1.1 identifies the same limit distributionally, giving the stated formula.

For $\epsilon>0$, let $\mathcal B_U^\epsilon f$ be the defining integral truncated to $t\ge\epsilon$. $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $1\le p<\infty$ there is
$C_{d,p}<\infty$ such that for all
$u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$,
$$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)} \le C_{d,p}|u|_{W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)},\qquad u_{\widehat S_d}:=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p<\infty$, integer $r\ge1$,
integer $s\ge0$, and real-valued $v\in W^{\max(r,s),p}(\widehat S_d)$.
There is a polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}(\widehat S_d)$, chosen by
matching all means $\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q=
\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha v$ for $|\alpha|\le r-1$, such that:

- if $0\le s\le r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le C|v|_{W^{r,p}(\widehat S_d)}$;
- if $s>r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le
  C\sum_{j=r}^{s}|v|_{W^{j,p}(\widehat S_d)}$.

The second clause assumes $v\in W^{s,p}$; constants depend only on
$d,p,r,s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Let F be complete for a multiplicative absolute value and V a finite-dimensional normed F-vector space. For any basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$, its coordinate sup norm $\|\sum a_iv_i\|_\infty=\max_i|a_i|$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the given norm. For $n=0$ both norms are zero. Consequently V is complete and every linear subspace is closed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

derivations.claim: On each reference facet, the P1 facet mass matrix is positive definite because $\int_Fp^2>0$ for every nonzero affine polynomial. Its inverse defines the dual functions $\widehat\psi_z$; affine scaling in [F2] gives $\|\psi_{z,F}\|_{L^2(F)}\le C h_F^{-(d-1)/2}$. The trace map in [F3] therefore makes every coefficient of $I_hv$ a bounded linear functional on the H1 trace of an adjacent cell. Shared coefficients define a continuous P1 function. If $v\in H^1_0$, [F4] makes all selected boundary-facet averages zero, so $I_hv$ has zero boundary nodal values and belongs to $H^1_0$ by [F1].

The coefficients reproduce every global affine polynomial: on the selected facet its trace is P1 and the dual moment equals its value at $z$. Shape regularity bounds the number of cells at each vertex: each simplex's vertex solid angle has a positive lower bound, while the total angle is at most $2\pi$ in dimension two or $4\pi$ in dimension three. The vertex-star graph is connected as follows. Choose a small chart cylinder meeting only cells incident to the vertex. At an interior vertex, a small ball lies in $D$. At a boundary vertex, the Lipschitz chart represents this local part of $D$ as the region above a Lipschitz graph; within a smaller base ball, vertical paths to a common height above the graph and a horizontal segment at that height connect any two points. Hence this local part is path connected. Join interior points of any two incident cells by a polygonal path there and perturb its finitely many segments to avoid the finite mesh skeleton of codimension at least two. The path then crosses only facet interiors and gives a facet-adjacency chain among cells incident to the vertex. Adjacent cell diameters are comparable by [F2]. Thus vertex-patch diameters and overlap are uniformly bounded.

Let $\omega_K$ be the union of cells meeting a vertex of $K$. Shape regularity bounds the number of cells at each vertex: each has a solid angle bounded below by the reference-cell shape bound, whereas the total angle is at most $2\pi$ in dimension two and $4\pi$ in dimension three. Each vertex-star graph is connected by step 1.2, and all stars of vertices of $K$ contain $K$, so their union is connected; neighboring cell diameters are comparable by [F2]. For adjacent cells $T,T'$ with common facet $F$, let $m_T,m_{T'}$ be their volume means. Cell Poincare and trace in [F3] give $\|w-m_T\|_{L^2(F)}\le Ch_K^{1/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(T)}$ and the analogous bound on $T'$. Since $|F|^{1/2}\asymp h_K^{(d-1)/2}$, it follows that $|m_T-m_{T'}|\le Ch_K^{(2-d)/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(T\cup T')}$. A path of bounded length through the patch graph then compares all cell means to one fixed $c_K$ and proves $\|w-c_K\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Applying the scaled trace estimate of [F3] and $\|\psi_{z,F_z}\|_{L^2(F_z)}\le Ch_K^{-(d-1)/2}$ gives $|\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}(w-c_K)|\le Ch_K^{1-d/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ for every vertex of $K$.

Suppose $v\in H^2(D)$. On each cell $T\subset\omega_K$, Bramble--Hilbert and affine scaling in [F2, F3] give $p_T\in P_1(T)$ with $\|v-p_T\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T)}$ and $\|
abla(v-p_T)\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T)}$. For adjacent cells $T,T\prime$ sharing a facet $F$, the scaled trace estimate applied to $v-p_T$ and its first derivatives gives $\|p_T-p_{T\prime}\|_{L^2(F)}\le Ch_K^{3/2}\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$ and $|F|^{1/2}|
abla p_T-
abla p_{T\prime}|\le Ch_K^{1/2}\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$. The second bound controls the full gradient difference, and the first then controls its constant part. Normalize both cell diameters by $h_K$. Shape regularity and comparability across the shared facet bound the normalized affine maps and their inverses; there are only finitely many vertex-orderings. Their closure is a compact set of nondegenerate reference-pair configurations. Finite-dimensional norm equivalence [F5] varies continuously on this compact set, so its constants are uniform; affine scaling then gives $\|p_T-p_{T\prime}\|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$. A bounded path through the connected cell-star graph lets one fixed cell polynomial $p\in P_1$ satisfy $\|v-p\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|
abla(v-p)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. This uses only local approximation and does not impose boundary values on $v$.

The reference P1 basis satisfies $\|\varphi_z\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{d/2}$ and $\|
abla\varphi_z\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{d/2-1}$. Since $I_h$ reproduces constants, step 2.1 bounds $\|I_hw-c_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|
abla I_hw\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Together with the patch Poincare bound for $w-c_K$, these prove the $L^2$ approximation and local H1 stability. Summing and using bounded overlap proves global H1-seminorm stability.

Facet duality reproduces every affine polynomial at every vertex, so $I_hp=p$ on $K$. Apply the local H1 stability from step 3.1 to $v-p$ and use step 2.2 to get $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Summing over cells and using the bounded patch overlap from step 3.1 proves the global H1 approximation estimate.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: On one $d$-simplex, $P_1(K)$ has the $d+1$ barycentric coordinate basis. The bubble $b_K$ is nonzero in the interior and vanishes at every vertex; because its polynomial degree is $d+1>1$, it is not in $P_1(K)$. Thus the scalar local velocity sum is direct with dimension $d+2$, and its $d$ vector components give $d(d+2)$. The local pressure dimension is $d+1$.

A continuous piecewise P1 scalar function is uniquely determined by its $N_v$ vertex values: affine uniqueness on each simplex proves injectivity, and assigning shared vertex values defines such a function by face-to-face conformity. Imposing zero trace sets exactly the $N_v-N_{v,0}$ boundary vertex values to zero, leaving $N_{v,0}$ independent velocity nodal values per component.

Each cell bubble is linearly independent of the nodal functions because its support interior is disjoint from every other cell bubble and it vanishes on the cell boundary, while a P1 polynomial vanishing on all vertices is zero. Hence the velocity dimension is $dN_{v,0}+dN_K$. The integral functional on $S_h^1$ is nonzero (it takes the positive value $|D|$ on $1$), so its zero-mean kernel has codimension one; therefore $\dim Q_h=N_v-1$.

statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular simplicial mesh, $d=2$ or $3$, mesh size $h=\max_Kh_K$. For each interior mesh vertex $z$, choose any incident facet $F_z$; for each boundary vertex choose an incident boundary facet. Let $\psi_{z,F_z}\in P_1(F_z)$ be the unique dual affine function satisfying $\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\varphi_y=\delta_{zy}$ for the facet's P1 nodal basis. Define
$$I_hv=\sum_z\left(\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\operatorname{tr}v\right)\varphi_z.$$
This is a linear face-average interpolant $H^1(D)\to S_h$, where $S_h$ is the continuous piecewise P1 space. It maps $H^1_0(D)$ into $S_h\cap H^1_0(D)$, is uniformly $H^1$-seminorm stable, and for each element patch $\omega_K$ has
$$\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$$
If $v\in H^2(D)$, then $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Constants depend only on dimension, the fixed domain, and the mesh shape-regularity bound. No point evaluation is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
